explanation: Ten single counters can be bundled as one ten; ten bundles of ten make one hundred. Draw a large square for each hundred, a line for each ten and a dot for each one. The size of a drawing does not change its agreed value. A collection of four hundreds, two tens and six ones represents 426.

A place-value chart keeps hundreds, tens and ones in separate columns. Write 426 = 400 + 20 + 6, reading four hundred and twenty-six. In 406 the zero records no tens; leaving its position out would give 46, a different quantity. Ten hundreds make 1000, one thousand.

Exchange without changing the total: 3 hundreds and 12 tens can become 4 hundreds and 2 tens. When a number is built in an unusual way, bundle groups of ten before writing its usual numeral. Check by adding the values, not by joining the spoken counts as digits.

explanation: Build two numbers with place-value bundles and compare hundreds first. If the hundreds match, compare tens; if those match, compare ones. For 618 and 681, six hundreds match but one ten is less than eight tens, so 618 < 681. A long numeral is not necessarily larger if both have the same number of digits.

A number line records order. For a pattern, describe what is added or removed at each step, then check the rule at every given jump. In a count by tens the ones digit stays fixed, but crossing a hundred can change two written digits. Do not copy just the last digit without checking the whole value.

Pair counters with no leftovers to model an even number. An odd number leaves one counter unpaired. Full tens can always be paired, so the ones digit decides: 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 mean even; 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 mean odd. Zero ones does not mean the whole number is zero.

explanation: Join two collections of base-ten pieces, keeping hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens and ones with ones. A part-whole bar shows the two addends as adjacent parts and the sum as the whole. Adding counts all the objects; the written columns record the same joining action.

When the ones total ten or more, exchange ten ones for one ten and keep the remaining ones. Add that new ten in the tens column. If the tens total ten or more, exchange ten tens for a hundred. The small carried digit represents a unit of the next place, not an extra one.

You may also break the second addend into hundreds, tens and ones and count on in useful jumps. Check the sum against the model: it must be at least as large as each nonnegative part. Subtracting one part from the sum should recover the other part. Keep all totals within 1000 this week.

explanation: A subtraction bar can show a whole split into a known part and a missing part. Start with the whole in base-ten pieces, remove the known part, and count what remains. A comparison bar instead aligns two amounts at the same start; the extra length is the difference. Both can lead to subtraction, but label what the answer counts.

If there are too few ones to remove, exchange a ten for ten ones. If there are no tens available, first exchange a hundred for ten tens. In 602, exchanging one hundred gives 5 hundreds, 10 tens, 2 ones; then exchanging one ten gives 5 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones. The value stays 602 throughout.

Never subtract the smaller digit from the larger digit in each column without respecting the whole operation. After finding a difference, add it to the removed part to recover the starting whole. For a story, also ask whether the answer should be a remaining amount, an extra amount, or a missing starting amount.

explanation: Make equal groups with 2 counters in each. Five such groups can be shown as five equal bar sections, each labelled 2, or as five rows of 2 dots. Counting all the counters gives 5 × 2 = 10. Here the first factor counts groups and the second says how many in each; label both quantities before calculating.

Build a new fact from a known one. If 4 × 2 = 8, another equal group gives 5 × 2 = 10. An array also lets you split a large group count into two easier counts. Keep every row the same length; unequal groups cannot be represented by one repeated-group multiplication statement.

Division reverses this grouping. Sharing 12 counters among 6 equal groups asks how many in each; making groups of 2 asks how many groups. Both use the same total but their answers name different things. Use a multiplication check: group count × group size must rebuild the total. All divisions here divide exactly, without leftovers.

explanation: Arrange counters in rows of five. Pair two five-counter rows to make one ten-counter row. This turns counting by fives into counting half as many groups of ten. explanation: Name one whole before naming a fraction. Imagine one paper strip divided into 2 equal-sized regions. One region is 1/2, read one half. The bottom number tells how many equal parts form the whole; the top number counts selected parts. Equal number of pieces is not enough if their sizes differ.

Shade parts of a complete strip and count them without changing their size. If a strip has two equal cells and both are selected, 2/2 names the whole. If a different strip has five equal cells and two are selected, the fraction is 2/5. The plain cells still belong to the whole and count in the denominator. For a unit fraction, exactly one equal part is selected. When equal wholes are split into more parts, each part becomes smaller. When the denominator stays fixed, more selected parts means more of the whole. Compare only after checking that the wholes have the same size; one half of a large cake need not equal one half of a small cake. No renaming to equivalent fractions is required here.

explanation: Compare unit fractions by placing equal whole strips side by side. One strip split into three equal parts gives larger single pieces than a strip split into six equal parts. The numerator one tells us that just one piece is selected. A greater denominator means more equal pieces were cut from the same whole, so that one selected piece is smaller. For example, 1/8 < 1/5. explanation: A clock face has sixty equal minute steps around its edge. The numbered marks are five minutes apart: at 1 the minute hand records 5 minutes past, at 2 it records 10, and so on. Count the smaller minute ticks after a known numbered mark to read the exact minute.

explanation: Before calculating, name the quantity: money, a time of day, or a duration. Model $1 with a hundred-cent bar and one hour with a sixty-minute bar. Both can be split into smaller units, but their exchange numbers are different; a common-looking pair of digits does not make the quantities interchangeable.

Read clock minutes by fives and extra ticks, but read a duration by counting complete sixty-minute groups. In a duration of 1 hour 8 minutes, eight is added to sixty. In $1.08, eight cents is added to one hundred cents. Labelled bars keep these meanings visible before writing either total.

Use comparison after expressing like quantities in the same unit. Money can be compared with money and durations with durations. A numerical answer without a unit can hide an incorrect exchange, so verify with the reverse grouping and say what the result describes. explanation: Length measures the distance from one endpoint to another. Lay a metre strip along a straight length, with no gaps or overlaps between repeated placements. The start must line up with zero; if the scale begins elsewhere, find the difference between endpoint readings. A metre, written m, suits room or playground lengths.

A drawn bar represents the measured length, not how heavy an object is. Align comparison bars at one end to see which extends farther. With measurements in the same unit, compare the numbers directly. A centimetre ruler suits a short pencil; a metre measure suits a classroom wall. Choose the unit to fit the object.

Read every interval on a supplied scale, including unlabelled marks. If consecutive labels differ by two metres with one intervening mark, each step is one metre. State the unit with each answer. The activity descriptions provide all readings; no physical measuring tool is required to solve them.

explanation: Mass describes how much matter an object contains and is measured using a balance or scale. A gram, written g, suits a small packet; a kilogram, written kg, suits heavier objects such as a filled schoolbag. Length alone does not decide mass: a small dense object can have more mass than a large light object.

On a balance, the lower pan holds the greater mass. Equal levels indicate equal masses. On a marked scale, find the size of one interval from the supplied labels before reading an unlabelled pointer position. Use a labelled bar to compare stated masses only when their units match.

This week keeps calculations within grams or within kilograms. Do not compare bare numbers such as 500 and 2 when their units differ; they count different-sized mass units. For these tasks choose a suitable unit or use the same-unit readings supplied. Compound-unit conversion is developed later.

explanation: Liquid volume measures how much liquid is present. A litre, written L, is a standard volume unit. Use repeated one-litre fills or a container with a litre scale. The shape or height of a container alone does not give its liquid volume; a tall narrow jug can hold the same amount as a short wide one.

Read the supplied scale at the liquid level. When scale marks are equally spaced, work out their interval first. A bar with sections labelled one litre can model a filled amount, a poured-out part and a remaining amount. Keep the unit L on every reading and result.

Pouring all liquid into another container without spilling does not change its volume. Adding or removing liquid does. Distinguish capacity, the most a container can hold, from its present contents. Tasks supply all capacities and readings, so predictions can be checked by comparing or combining litre amounts.

weeks.title: Choosing measures and checking readings
weeks.objective: Select suitable measurement tools and reason with labelled length, mass and volume data.

connection.before: Read litre scales and compare liquid volumes without relying on container shape.
connection.after: P3 combines units and converts between larger and smaller units.

days: Explore choosing measures and checking readings with objects or the fully described models; say what each unit represents.
Rebuild the first worked example; draw and label its parts before writing the equation.
Compare the two worked examples and complete worksheet A, explaining one answer aloud.
Use worksheet B to connect representations and repair errors; check quantities with another method.
Choose worksheet C applications; explain a solution and revisit an error from earlier in the week.
explanation: First decide which attribute is being measured. Distance along a rope needs a length unit and a ruler or tape. The mass of a parcel needs a balance or scale. The amount of liquid needs a measuring container. Labels such as m, g, kg and L identify the attribute and prevent unlike quantities from being combined.

Draw same-attribute quantities as labelled bars when adding parts, removing amounts or comparing measurements. Read a scale by finding equal interval sizes before locating the pointer. In a data list, compare only quantities given in the same unit; a large numerical reading in grams cannot be compared directly with a small reading in kilograms.

Check a result against the situation. A remainder cannot exceed the starting amount after removal; a container must have capacity at least its contents. An estimate can be plausible without being exact, but these tasks give exact readings for calculation. Describe the measurement procedure so another learner could repeat it without gaps, overlaps or an incorrect starting point.

examples.prompt: A box is 4 kg, a rope is 4 m and a jug holds 4 L. Do these matching numbers mean matching measurements?
steps: Kilograms describe the box mass.

explanation: Handle or imagine a solid box and turn it to see the surfaces hidden from the front. A cube has six equal square faces. A cuboid has six rectangular faces; a cube is the special case in which those faces are all equal squares. In sorting tasks, use cube as the most specific name when all six equal square faces are stated.

A flat drawing shows only a view of a solid. A square outline could be one face of a cube, but the outline alone does not prove that the whole object is a cube. Use the complete supplied description of the object. Colour, decoration and how the object is turned do not change its solid type.

Flat faces allow boxes to rest on a face and stack in a stable way when aligned. Compare cubes and other cuboids using face shapes rather than object names alone; an everyday box can have many proportions. No net drawing is required here. Text descriptions explicitly state the shape features needed for classification.

explanation: A sphere has a completely curved surface, like an ideal ball, and no flat face. A cylinder has two equal flat circular ends joined by a curved surface. A cone has one flat circular base, a curved surface and a pointed tip. Ideal descriptions matter: a real object may have a rim, handle or opening not part of the simple solid model.

Turn the solid or read every surface description before sorting it. A circular outline alone might be the end of a cylinder, the base of a cone or the view of a sphere. A surface-based description separates these possibilities. Use a circle for a flat shape and sphere for the solid ball form.

Movement depends on how a solid is placed. A cylinder can roll on its curved side or stand on a flat end. A cone can stand on its base and roll along a curved path on its side. A sphere can roll and has no flat face to stand on. Explain the relevant surface rather than saying every round-looking object behaves the same way.

explanation: A picture graph replaces repeated objects with symbols. Read the key before counting: if one symbol stands for two objects, three symbols stand for three pairs, or six objects. You can build this with three pairs of counters and then replace each pair with one drawn icon.

explanation: The graph key determines the value of each symbol. One symbol for ten objects lets a large count use fewer marks. Build ten-object bundles to model the key, then place one symbol for every complete bundle. With whole symbols only, a ten-unit key can show counts such as twenty or fifty exactly.

The same underlying data can be redrawn with a different key. A row representing forty objects uses four ten-unit symbols or eight five-unit symbols. The number of drawn marks changes but the object count does not. To compare two graphs with different keys, convert each row to objects first.

A graph without its key does not state a unique object count. More symbols on one graph need not mean more objects than fewer symbols on another graph with a larger key. Explain both the symbol count and the value per symbol when justifying a reading or a redraw.

explanation: A planning question begins by translating every needed graph row into objects. With one symbol for four kits, a row of five symbols means twenty kits. Draw one equal-part bar per category, label each four-kit part, and write the totals before combining categories or comparing a supply.

Choose operations according to the question. Joining categories needs addition; finding a shortage needs subtraction; making equal packs needs division; supplying several equal groups needs multiplication. A two-step plan should label the intermediate result so that a count of kits is not confused with a count of symbols or children.

Check that a proposed plan meets all stated conditions. Enough supplies means available quantity is at least the amount required, and an exact order must match it with none left. Use inverse calculations or an alternative graph count to verify. These fictional data support decisions about this plan only, not claims about real classes.

examples.prompt: A graph has 3 symbols for brushes and 2 for sponges; one symbol is 4 items. How many items are there altogether?

Five total symbols times four also gives twenty items.
